blocks.text: Imagine a factory assembly line where each worker performs a specific task. How can this concept improve the performance of a computer processor?

blocks.markdown: Pipelining is a technique used in computer architecture to increase instruction throughput. By overlapping the execution of multiple instructions, pipelining allows a processor to work on several instructions simultaneously, similar to how an assembly line operates.

blocks.title: Pipelining
blocks.text: Pipelining is a method where multiple instruction phases are overlapped to improve instruction throughput without reducing the execution time of individual instructions.

blocks.markdown: A pipeline is divided into stages, each responsible for a part of the instruction execution process. Common stages include instruction fetch, decode, execute, memory access, and write-back. Each stage processes a different instruction simultaneously, allowing for increased throughput.

blocks.markdown: While pipelining improves throughput, it introduces hazards that can stall the pipeline. These include data hazards, control hazards, and structural hazards.

blocks.title: Types of Hazards
blocks.text: Data hazards occur when instructions depend on the results of previous instructions. Control hazards arise from branch instructions. Structural hazards occur when hardware resources are insufficient.

blocks.title: Pipeline Stalls
blocks.text: Hazards can cause pipeline stalls, reducing the effective throughput. Techniques like forwarding and branch prediction can mitigate these effects.
